summary: Clarifies and updates a single sentence in RFC 3979 about third-party intellectual property disclosures. When someone else files a disclosure, the IETF Executive Director is to notify the IPR holder and ask whether they have any disclosure to make. It is a best current practice, later replaced by RFC 8179.

eli5.summary: If someone else says your invention is part of a project, the project's manager tells you and asks if you have anything to add. This note makes that rule clear.

questions: what is a third party ipr disclosure
how does the ietf handle third party ipr disclosures
what does rfc 4879 change in rfc 3979
who does the ietf ask for licensing assurance
subtitle: A one-word fix to the IETF patent disclosure rules: ask the IPR holder, not the discloser.

tldr.problem: RFC 3979 says the IETF Executive Director asks the 'discloser' of an IPR disclosure for a licensing assurance. When a third party made the disclosure, that person does not own the IPR and cannot promise licensing terms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC changes the word 'discloser' to 'holder' in Section 4 (C) of RFC 3979, so the Executive Director notifies the IPR holder and asks them whether they have any disclosure to make.
tldr.outcome: This is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 3979. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 8179.

today: RFC 4879 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 8179. It updated RFC 3979.

sections.title: A Single-Sentence Clarification
sections.content:
This document clarifies and updates a single sentence in RFC 3979. It concerns third party Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) disclosures, where someone other than the owner tells the IETF that a technology may be covered by IPR.

The intention is that the IETF Executive Director notifies the IPR holder that a third party disclosure has been filed, and asks the holder whether they have any disclosure that needs to be made under the applicable RFC 3979 rules.
sections.eli5: Sometimes someone else says a project uses your invention. This note says the project's manager must tell you, the owner, and ask what you want to say.

sections.title: The Fix to Section 4 (C)
sections.content:
Section 4 (C) of RFC 3979 says that once IPR has been disclosed for IETF documents, the Executive Director shall request from the discloser a written assurance. The assurance says that, once the IESG approves the specification for publication as an RFC, all persons will be able to obtain the right to implement, use and distribute the technology under one of the licensing options in Section 6.5 of RFC 3979, unless such a statement has already been submitted.

The RFC points out the flaw. In the case of third party disclosures, it makes no sense to ask the discloser about potential licensing terms, since they do not own the IPR. It only makes sense to ask the IPR holder.

The change is exactly one word: "discloser" becomes "holder" in that text.
sections.eli5: You cannot promise to share something you do not own. So the question goes to whoever owns it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document states that it has no known security implications. It changes only who is asked for a licensing assurance in an administrative procedure.
sections.eli5: This is a paperwork fix, so it does not make anything less safe.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Intellectual Property Rights in IETF Technology", BCP 79, RFC 3979, March 2005.
